body:
Foundation of the Prarthana Samaj

The Prarthana Samaj was founded in Bombay on 31 March 1867 by Dr Atmaram Pandurang. It emerged in an environment where educated Indians were questioning caste restrictions, unequal opportunities for women and practices defended through religious authority.

The movement was influenced by reform currents from Bengal, especially the activities and visits of Keshab Chandra Sen. However, Sen should not be identified as its founder. Atmaram Pandurang founded the organisation, while Mahadev Govind Ranade and Ramakrishna Gopal Bhandarkar became important figures in its development.

Earlier reform activity in Bombay had included the Paramhansa Mandali, whose members opposed caste distinctions and questioned established religious practices. Some people associated with that earlier movement later participated in the Prarthana Samaj.

Religious principles and Bhakti influence

The word prarthana means prayer. The Samaj emphasised worship of one formless God, moral conduct and spiritual equality. Its own worship did not depend on image worship or elaborate priestly ritual.

The organisation drew inspiration from the Bhakti tradition of Maharashtra, including the devotional teachings of saints such as Namdev and Tukaram. This connection helped its members express reform through familiar Indian religious language rather than simply adopting a foreign model.

Prarthana Samaj members also sought truth in different religious traditions. They did not regard any single scripture as entirely infallible. Their religious outlook therefore differed from the Arya Samaj's later insistence upon the supreme authority of the Vedas.

The social reform programme

The Samaj linked religious belief with practical improvement in society. Four important concerns were:

  • Caste restrictions: Opposition to discrimination and rigid barriers between social groups.
  • Widow remarriage: Support for the right of widows to marry again without social exclusion.
  • Women's education: Encouragement of education for girls and women.
  • Child marriage: Criticism of marriage at an early age and support for changes in social practice.

Its members believed that belief in one God and the spiritual worth of human beings should encourage more equal treatment in society. However, reformist declarations did not automatically remove the influence of caste customs or conservative family expectations.

The Gujarat connection

Gujarat had its own early history of organised social and religious discussion. The Manav Dharma Sabha was established at Surat in 1844, with Durgaram Manchharam Mehta and Dadoba Pandurang associated with its foundation. It sought to examine religious beliefs and social customs through reason and ethical principles.

The Manav Dharma Sabha must not be confused with the Prarthana Samaj. The former was established at Surat in 1844; the latter originated in Bombay in 1867. The Prarthana Samaj subsequently developed branches in several places, including Surat and Ahmedabad.

Founder versus influence: Keshab Chandra Sen influenced the development of the Prarthana Samaj, but its founder was Atmaram Pandurang. Ranade and Bhandarkar were prominent leaders, not substitutes for the founding name.

Prelims focus

  • 31 March 1867: Prarthana Samaj founded by Atmaram Pandurang in Bombay.
  • M. G. Ranade and R. G. Bhandarkar were important associated reformers.
  • The movement drew on the Maharashtra Bhakti tradition, especially Namdev and Tukaram.
  • Its concerns included caste restrictions, widow remarriage, women's education and child marriage.
  • 1844: Manav Dharma Sabha established at Surat; Prarthana Samaj later had branches at Surat and Ahmedabad.
  • Trap: Manav Dharma Sabha and Prarthana Samaj are distinct organisations with different founding places and years.

[Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Mumbai Legacy Project: Prarthana Samaj, pp. 1–2, consulted 20 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 8, Caste and Social Reform, printed p. 100; National Institute of Open Schooling, History (315), lesson 18, Reform Movements in Western India, printed pp. 31–32; University of Mumbai, History of Modern Maharashtra, section 5.2 on Dadoba Pandurang and Manav Dharma Sabha, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: A prayer gathering represents the devotional and social character of the Prarthana Samaj.

title: Prarthana Samaj and Socio-Religious Reform in Western India

body:
Dayanand Saraswati and his Gujarat origin

Swami Dayanand Saraswati (1824–1883) was the founder of the Arya Samaj. He was born at Tankara in present-day Gujarat, in the Kathiawar region. His original name was Mool Shankar. Tankara is an important Gujarat connection for questions about the origins of modern Indian socio-religious reform.

Dayanand examined prevailing Hindu religious practices and argued that many customs should be judged against what he considered the original teachings of the Vedas. He believed that returning to those teachings would restore religious truth and support a better social order.

Foundation of Arya Samaj

Dayanand founded the Arya Samaj at Bombay in 1875. His major work, Satyarth Prakash, was also first published in 1875. Its title is commonly translated as The Light of Truth.

The central message of the movement is usually expressed as Back to the Vedas. This was a call to recover the religious authority and principles that Dayanand believed were found in the earliest Vedic teachings. It did not mean that the organisation rejected every aspect of modern education or every form of social change.

Vedic authority and religious criticism

The Arya Samaj treated the Vedas as the supreme and infallible source of religious truth, when correctly interpreted. Dayanand taught belief in one God and rejected the idea that image worship was necessary for genuine worship.

He criticised several practices that he believed had departed from Vedic teaching:

  • Idolatry: Worship directed towards images or idols rather than the formless God.
  • Polytheism: Religious belief centred on many separate gods rather than one supreme divine reality.
  • Elaborate ritualism: Practices that placed excessive weight on rituals instead of religious understanding and moral conduct.
  • Priestly domination: Claims that religious truth could be understood only through the authority of particular hereditary priestly groups.

Dayanand's approach was therefore revivalist in its appeal to Vedic origins and reformist in its criticism of contemporary practices. Opposition to idolatry did not make the Arya Samaj identical to the Brahmo Samaj: the movements differed particularly over the status of the Vedas.

The Arya Samaj's social programme

Dayanand and his followers connected religious reform with changes in everyday social life. They criticised caste status determined solely by birth and argued for a social order in which qualities and conduct were more important than inherited rank.

The movement also opposed child marriage, supported widow remarriage and promoted education for girls and women. Its educational work later became one of its most visible public activities.

These ideas challenged both the assumptions of some colonial and missionary critics and the position of defenders of existing religious customs. The Arya Samaj claimed that the solution to social problems lay in a properly understood Vedic tradition.

Place distinction: Dayanand Saraswati was born at Tankara in Gujarat in 1824, but he established the Arya Samaj at Bombay in 1875. A question may ask either the birthplace of the founder or the place where the organisation began.

Prelims focus

  • 1824: Dayanand Saraswati was born at Tankara in present-day Gujarat.
  • His original name was Mool Shankar.
  • 1875: Arya Samaj founded at Bombay.
  • 1875: Satyarth Prakash was first published.
  • The central religious message was Back to the Vedas; the Samaj upheld Vedic authority and rejected image worship.
  • Trap: Calling for Vedic revival did not prevent the Arya Samaj from supporting social reform and education.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 97–99; National Institute of Open Schooling, History (315), lesson 18, Arya Samaj, printed pp. 32–34; Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook: Rajkot, Village and Town Directory section, Dayanand Saraswati Birth Place, printed p. 123; Vanya Vaidehi Bhargav, Arya Samaj, Oxford Bibliographies in Hinduism, Introduction, published 7 January 2025, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Arya Samaj's Vedic foundation made it revivalist, while inspiring criticism of religious practices and a programme of social reform.
pictures.caption: The Vedas formed the religious foundation for the Arya Samaj's reform programme.

title: Swami Dayanand Saraswati and the Vedic Principles of Arya Samaj

body:
How the Arya Samaj expanded

Although the Arya Samaj began in Bombay in 1875, its influence became particularly strong in northern India. A branch was established at Lahore in 1877, and Punjab became an important centre of its activities.

The movement used preaching, public discussion, printed publications and educational institutions to spread its ideas. Dayanand's use of Hindi helped communicate his message beyond people educated in Sanskrit or English.

Shuddhi: religious reconversion

Shuddhi refers to a process of religious purification or reconversion through which people who had adopted another religion were brought into, or restored to, the Hindu religious community as understood by the Arya Samaj.

The Shuddhi movement reflected the Arya Samaj's concern about conversion to Christianity and Islam and its effort to strengthen the Hindu religious community. It was a religious and social campaign, not a school or a separate educational society.

Shuddhi also became connected with the question of who could be included within Hindu society, especially when inherited caste restrictions had excluded groups from full religious participation. At the same time, reconversion campaigns could sharpen competition and tensions between religious communities.

The Dayanand Anglo-Vedic educational approach

After Dayanand's death in 1883, followers sought to establish institutions that could continue his teachings. The Dayanand Anglo-Vedic Trust and Management Society was established at Lahore in 1886. A school began there in the same year, with Lala Hansraj as its principal.

The term Dayanand Anglo-Vedic (DAV) describes an educational approach combining aspects of English and modern learning with Vedic religious and moral instruction. The DAV institutions demonstrated that an organisation committed to Vedic revival could also make use of modern educational methods.

The Gurukul approach

Not all Arya Samaj leaders agreed about the appropriate balance between English education and Sanskrit or Vedic learning. Some wanted religious education to follow a more traditional residential model.

These disagreements contributed to an organisational division in 1893 between the DAV or College group and the Gurukul group. Both remained within the wider Arya Samaj tradition, but they supported different educational priorities.

Munshi Ram, later known as Swami Shraddhanand, established Gurukul Kangri near Haridwar in 1902. Its educational approach placed greater emphasis on residential study, Sanskrit and Vedic teaching.

FeatureDAV approachGurukul approach
Main emphasisModern and Vedic education togetherSanskrit and Vedic residential education
Associated leaderLala HansrajMunshi Ram, later Swami Shraddhanand
Important institutionDAV school, Lahore, 1886Gurukul Kangri, 1902

The educational differences should not obscure the organisations' shared religious foundation. Both approaches sought to spread Arya Samaj ideals, while disagreeing about the best institutional form for education.

Education as a method of social reform

Arya Samaj institutions helped extend schooling, including education for girls and members of communities facing caste exclusion. Education was regarded as a way to spread religious understanding, strengthen social organisation and improve opportunities.

Its activities therefore had several dimensions: religious revival through Vedic teachings, social reform through criticism of discriminatory practices, and institution-building through schools and related organisations.

Prelims focus

  • 1877: Lahore Arya Samaj was established.
  • Shuddhi was associated with religious reconversion, not with a particular school.
  • 1886: DAV educational organisation and school at Lahore; Lala Hansraj was the school's principal.
  • 1893: Organisational division associated with differences over education.
  • 1902: Gurukul Kangri established near Haridwar by Munshi Ram, later Swami Shraddhanand.
  • Trap: DAV and Gurukul institutions differed in educational emphasis, but both were associated with the Arya Samaj.

[National Institute of Open Schooling, History (315), lesson 18, Arya Samaj, printed pp. 32–34; Vanya Vaidehi Bhargav, Arya Samaj, Oxford Bibliographies in Hinduism, Introduction and discussion of Arya Samaj and education, published 7 January 2025, consulted 20 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 97–99.]

title: Arya Samaj in Practice: Shuddhi, DAV Education and Gurukuls
